cover#0: This is the Tecolutla field: a small El Abra reef on the Golden Lane trend in northern Veracruz, discovered by PEMEX in 1956. What you are looking at is the top of the reef, mapped from the 2019 seismic grid and coloured from blue on the flanks to red at the crest, with every well drilled on it.
cover#1: Over the next half hour we will walk through where the field sits, how it was found and produced well by well, what the reservoir and its fluids are, what it costs to run, and why one more well, TEC-12, at the crest is the opportunity. The presentation plays itself; you can pause, step back, or open the 3-D field and the data tables from the tabs at the top at any time.
goldenlane#0: Start with the setting. In the Cretaceous, a reef grew round the edge of the Tuxpan platform: an atoll about a hundred and fifty kilometres long. That rim is the Golden Lane, the Faja de Oro, and it has given Mexico some of its most famous wells.
goldenlane#1: Uplift and erosion at the end of the Albian cut the rim into separate blocks, each a reef build-up sealed by Tertiary shale. Every Golden Lane field is one of those blocks.
goldenlane#2: The trend made its name early. Cerro Azul number four, about a hundred and ten kilometres north-west of here, blew out in February 1916 and flowed uncontrolled for nine days at an estimated two hundred and sixty thousand barrels a day, one of the largest wells ever drilled. It went on to make more than fifty seven million barrels in fourteen years. Same reef; very different scale.
goldenlane#3: Tecolutla is at the south-eastern tip of the onshore rim, about sixty kilometres from Poza Rica and seven from the coast. It was licensed in Round 1.3 in 2016. The adjacent TM-01 block, with its own El Abra pools, was offered in Round 2.3 in 2018 and went to Jaguar after a tie-break cash bonus of twenty six point one million dollars.
goldenlane#4: Against its neighbours it is small and thin: about two and a half million barrels in place per square kilometre, against a reef-rim median of eight. That sets the scale for everything that follows. This is a field where one good well matters.
glance#0: Here is the field in six numbers.
glance#1: Nine wells. Five of them produced oil: TEC-2, 6, 7 and 9 under PEMEX, and TEC-10 under Tonalli. Together they made about two million barrels, with the field peaking at nine hundred and thirty two barrels a day in March 1972.
glance#2: Seven point eight to eleven million barrels in place, so about a fifth to a quarter recovered. The pressure has barely moved in sixty years because an aquifer replaces what is produced. And the highest El Abra on the seismic, at the planned TEC-12 bottom hole, has never had a well produce from it.
structure#0: This is the top of the El Abra reef from the 2019 depth grid, coloured blue on the deep flanks to red at the highest point. The field is an elongated north-west to south-east high, faulted on both flanks, with Tertiary shale resting directly on the reef.
structure#1: The wells tie the map to within two metres. TEC-6 and TEC-9 are the highest wells, at about two thousand two hundred and ninety five metres subsea. TEC-2 is at the north end, TEC-7 on the east flank, and TEC-10, drilled in 2018, came in lower to the south-west. TEC-101, TEC-3 and TEC-5 define the flanks.
structure#2: The dashed blue line is the lowest known oil at minus two thousand three hundred and seventy four metres, from a 1956 drill-stem test in TEC-3. It closes around the whole structure.
structure#3: And the star is TEC-12: a short deviated well from the TEC-10 pad to the southern high, between TEC-6, TEC-9 and TEC-10, where the reef is highest.
seismic#0: Can we trust that map at the crest? We read the full PEMEX pre-stack time migration and the 2019 depth migration. This is an inline through the planned TEC-12 bottom hole, with the reef top grid draped over it.
seismic#1: On the PSTM we tracked the reef-top event across all fourteen thousand traces of the field and tied it to six wells. Time follows the well tops, with a correlation of plus point seven.
seismic#2: Converted with the crestal wells’ own velocities, the reef top at TEC-12 is at minus two thousand two hundred and ninety three metres, give or take four. That is three metres above TEC-9 and seventeen above TEC-10. Ninety seven percent of the field is lower in time; only TEC-6 is higher.
seismic#3: The depth migration looks sharper, but its strongest reflector is the top of the carbonate package, not the reef. A marl sits on the reef and thickens off the crest, which is the next slide.
marl#0: People ask what the marl is and why it keeps coming up. This is a correlation panel across the field, hung on sea level. Blue is the El Abra reef; brown is the Tantoyuca marl, an Eocene shale that buried the eroded reef top.
marl#1: Now add the depth window that TEC-12 targets, two thousand two hundred and ninety four to two thousand three hundred and eleven metres. At the crest, at TEC-6, TEC-9 and TEC-12, that window is reef. At TEC-10 and TEC-101, where the reef top is lower, the same depths are still marl.
marl#2: The rock tells them apart. The TEC-10 cuttings in the window are a third quartz with clay and pyrite; the reef is almost pure calcite.
marl#3: On logs the marl reads about five ohm-metres, seventy one microseconds per foot on the sonic and a photo-electric factor near four. El Abra reads sixteen to forty seven ohm-metres, fifty two to fifty seven microseconds and above five.
marl#4: So when someone says TEC-10’s upper zone was wet, the answer is that TEC-10 never had El Abra at those depths. It drilled marl. The same depths at the crest are reef, and that is what TEC-12 goes to measure.
history#0: Watch the field build up in time. In 1956 PEMEX drilled five wells in a year. TEC-3, the first, found oil over salt water low on the north-east flank. TEC-2 discovered the field in June at four hundred and fifty barrels a day. TEC-5 found the reef far too low. TEC-6 and TEC-7 came in at five hundred barrels a day each.
history#1: Within months salt water reached TEC-2 and TEC-7, which had been completed low in the column, and both were shut in. For fourteen years TEC-6 carried the field alone, at about a hundred barrels a day, and the 1964 pressure surveys still read the discovery pressure.
history#2: In late 1971 PEMEX worked over all three wells and moved each one ten to twenty five metres up the column, away from the water. In March 1972 the field peaked at nine hundred and thirty two barrels a day. TEC-101 found the west flank wet, and in 1973 TEC-9 was drilled on the southern high.
history#3: For the next quarter century four wells produced together. Water cut climbed everywhere, and the wells were cycled on and off to let the water cones settle. TEC-6 moved up a second time in 1976. By the 1980s each well made twenty five to forty barrels a day, yet a 1998 pressure survey still showed no depletion.
history#4: From 1999 PEMEX wound the field down. TEC-6 and TEC-7 last produced in 2006, and TEC-6 was abandoned with a parted casing. In 2012 a cheap solvent and acid job lifted TEC-9 from ten to a hundred barrels a day, which is damage, not depletion, but PEMEX plugged it a year later. TEC-2 made the last PEMEX oil in 2016.
history#5: In late 2016 PEMEX handed the field to Tonalli. In 2018 Tonalli cleaned out TEC-2 and drilled TEC-10, which tested a hundred and ninety four barrels a day and measured almost the discovery pressure. The horizontal TEC-11 made only water and was plugged, and TEC-7 was converted to take the field’s produced water.
history#6: Through 2020 and 2021 TEC-10, with TEC-2 at times, made thirty to seventy barrels a day at high water cut, kept going with solvent treatments for wax. The field was shut in in February 2022 after the regulator rejected the evaluation report. TEC-10 was stimulated and restarted in November, and the last oil was produced in January 2023.
history#7: And that brings us to today. Nothing is producing. TEC-10 can be brought back on a solvent-treatment schedule, and TEC-2 can produce intermittently alongside it. TEC-7 is the disposal well. Every PEMEX producer except TEC-2 is plugged. About one point seven million barrels are in the monthly record, nearly two million with PEMEX’s early allocations, and the crest of the reef is still untouched.
w-TEC-6#0: Now the wells one at a time, starting with the biggest producer. TEC-6 was completed in October 1956, open hole at the bottom of its reef section, and flowed about five hundred barrels a day with three percent water.
w-TEC-6#1: From 1957 it carried the field alone for fourteen years, at about a hundred barrels a day.
w-TEC-6#2: In 1971 PEMEX squeezed the original interval and moved up to two thousand three hundred and twenty four metres, then in 1976 up again, to two thousand three hundred and fourteen. Each move bought a new peak, the second at nearly three hundred barrels a day in 1977.
w-TEC-6#3: It produced until 2006 and was abandoned in 2007 with its casing parted at three hundred and fifty two metres. It sits beside the TEC-10 pad that TEC-12 will be drilled from, which is why anti-collision is in the programme. In all, about nine hundred thousand barrels.
w-TEC-2#0: TEC-2 discovered the field. Its first test, at the very top of El Abra, flowed gas-rich oil: possible evidence of a small gas cap at the crest in 1956. It was completed lower down, at four hundred and fifty three barrels a day.
w-TEC-2#1: Nine months later salt water arrived and it was shut in for fifteen years. In December 1971 it was recompleted thirty metres higher and produced from that interval until 2016: three hundred and twenty thousand barrels.
w-TEC-2#2: In 2018 Tonalli found the tubing full of paraffin. The well test showed a skin of plus one hundred and ninety six: the well is badly damaged near the wellbore, not depleted. A plug in 2019 shut off the wet deeper perforations.
w-TEC-2#3: Its last production was sixteen barrels a day in January 2023, after a December workover. It is a low-rate, intermittent well, cycled on and off to let the water cone settle. It pays when it shares costs with TEC-10, and GLJ carries it as non-producing with a small workover.
w-TEC-7#0: TEC-7 tested five hundred and sixty barrels a day in January 1957. Its electric log, run before any production, is the best evidence we have about the top of the reef: the top seven metres at thirteen percent water saturation and seventeen percent porosity.
w-TEC-7#1: It watered out in seven weeks from its low completion and was shut in until 1971.
w-TEC-7#2: Recompleted twenty five metres higher in October 1971, it came back at nearly five hundred barrels a day and was the biggest contributor to the 1972 peak. It produced until 1990, then briefly in 2006.
w-TEC-7#3: In 2019 Tonalli reopened it and got only water, a hundred and eighty two barrels a day, probably through bad cement to the old perforations. It became the field’s water-injection well, which is what cut the operating cost by two thirds.
w-TEC-9#0: TEC-9 was drilled in 1973 as a deviated well onto the southern high, a hundred and eighteen metres from the TEC-12 bottom hole.
w-TEC-9#1: From one interval it made three hundred and fifty three thousand barrels over almost forty years. Its 1973 logs show the top eight metres of the reef porous, at about fifteen percent, and at the same saturation as the producing interval. PEMEX cemented that top unit behind casing and never perforated it.
w-TEC-9#2: In 2012, at ten barrels a day, PEMEX ran solvent and three cubic metres of acid and the rate jumped to a hundred and two barrels a day. That is near-wellbore damage, not depletion, the same story as TEC-2 and TEC-10.
w-TEC-9#3: A workover that November failed, and the well was plugged in January 2013. Its unperforated top is TEC-12’s best analogue.
w-TEC-3#0: Three wells never produced, and they matter because they define the edges. TEC-3, the very first well, found the reef at minus two thousand three hundred and seventy three metres on the north-east flank. Its drill-stem test recovered oil over salt water: that is the lowest known oil in the field, minus two thousand three hundred and seventy four.
w-TEC-3#1: TEC-5, a kilometre and a half to the north-west, found the reef two hundred and fifty metres lower, off the structure.
w-TEC-3#2: TEC-101 in 1972 found the west flank water-invaded at minus two thousand three hundred and thirty four, with the same low-resistivity marl above the reef that TEC-10 later found. All three are plugged.
w-TEC-10#0: TEC-10 is Tonalli’s well, drilled in 2018 from the TEC-6 pad to the south-west. It was cored, fully logged, and tested in three zones. The deeper two gave no oil. The top zone, just below the reef top, flowed a hundred and ninety four barrels a day after stimulation.
w-TEC-10#1: It peaked at two hundred and thirty two barrels a day in October 2018 and declined to seventy seven within a year, with water cut rising from forty to two thirds. Wax was dropping out in the tubing, and four solvent jobs in 2019 kept it going.
w-TEC-10#2: By the end of 2021 it was making thirty four barrels a day at eighty six percent water. After the 2022 shut-in a twenty-thousand-dollar stimulation brought it back at about forty five barrels a day net, and it last produced in January 2023.
w-TEC-10#3: The reservoir behind it was at full pressure in 2018, so the decline between treatments is wax and near-wellbore restriction. TEC-10 should come back at thirty to forty five barrels a day on a regular solvent or hot-oil schedule, which is how GLJ carries it, and that is the base the incremental TEC-12 economics stand on.
tec11-concept#0: TEC-11 is the well people remember, so it deserves a careful explanation. Start with the problem it was meant to solve. Every vertical well in this field drew the bottom water up into a cone around its perforations and watered out.
tec11-concept#1: A horizontal well at the top of the column spreads the same production along seven hundred metres of hole. Drawdown at any point is small, so the water rises slowly and evenly instead of coning.
tec11-concept#2: If it worked, it would change the field: the January 2019 plan carried three horizontals at six hundred and ninety four barrels a day each, against a hundred and fifty for TEC-10.
tec11-concept#3: The important point for TEC-12 is that this concept was never actually tested. Here is what happened.
tec11-failures#0: This is TEC-11 along its length. The horizontal axis is measured depth along the hole, the vertical is depth below sea level. The dashed blue line is the top of El Abra from the 2019 grid along the well path, and the coloured line is the well itself.
tec11-failures#1: Colour comes from the sonic log recorded while drilling. Tan is marl-like, blue is reef-like. Almost the whole lateral reads like the marl, seventy three microseconds per foot, and it ran four to ten metres above the mapped reef top. No resistivity was run to check, so this is an interpretation, but the sonic, the grid and the tops table agree. The lateral probably never got into the reef it was aimed at.
tec11-failures#2: Then the completion went wrong in sequence. The liner hanger was damaged and the tie-back failed. In May 2019 a bit and mill were lost in the hole at two thousand eight hundred and sixty six metres, cutting off the last four hundred metres of open hole.
tec11-failures#3: Because the selective tool could not pass the damaged hanger, five short intervals were perforated and acid was pumped from surface with no isolation. Pressure broke down at once: the acid most likely opened a fracture to the aquifer.
tec11-failures#4: The well then made two hundred and sixty to two hundred and eighty six barrels a day of water with traces of oil. In August the lateral was plugged off.
tec11-failures#5: A question that comes up: why not produce the Tantoyuca instead? It was tested above the plug at the end of August 2019, perforated at two thousand three hundred and sixty one to two thousand three hundred and sixty four metres. In four and a half days on a fourteen sixty-fourths choke it flowed only water, a hundred and ninety two barrels a day at first and ninety six at the end, five hundred and twenty eight barrels in all, with no measurable oil. Only a trace of heavy, seventeen-degree oil was sampled. The Tantoyuca here is a tight marl, three to six ohm-metres with no fractures; there is no stabilised oil rate to report because there was none.
tec11-failures#6: So TEC-11 tested how fast the aquifer reaches a well through acidised fractures. It did not test a horizontal in reservoir rock. The lessons are built into TEC-12: a conventional well, a full log suite before completion, perforation on the data, and no unisolated acid near the water.
tec11-failures#7: All in, it cost four point four million dollars against a three point nine million budget, including about a million of completion invoices whose status is still unresolved.
performance#0: Here is the whole production record, by well, as a monthly rate. One caveat first: there is no monthly record at all for 1956 to 1959, the hatched band. Those years survive only as PEMEX wellfile allocations, so the chart starts in 1960. From 1960 to 1965 there is a single field-level record, which is TEC-6, the only producer at the time. Where the rate drops to zero, the well was reported shut in.
performance#1: Five wells produced oil. TEC-6 made about nine hundred thousand barrels, TEC-2 and TEC-9 about three hundred and fifty thousand each, TEC-7 about three hundred thousand, and TEC-10, in four years, seventy seven thousand. The peak was nine hundred and thirty two barrels a day in March 1972, from three wells right after their recompletions.
performance#2: The pattern is the same in every well: strong initial rates, water arriving from below, a recompletion higher up, and a new peak. Water ended each well. Pressure never did.
performance#3: And late in life the decline is damage, not depletion. Wax and skin choke the wells, and cheap solvent and acid jobs brought TEC-9 back in 2012 and kept TEC-10 going. That matters for running the field, and for TEC-12.
pressure#0: This is the single most important reservoir fact. Here is every pressure measurement in the field since 1956, corrected to one datum, on a scale that starts at zero. Discovery pressure was twenty four point six five megapascals. In 2018, after sixty two years, TEC-2 and TEC-10 both measured twenty four point one four. Half a megapascal. Two percent.
pressure#1: The grey points are flowing pressures or very short shut-ins, which read low and are not reservoir pressure.
pressure#2: To see what that means, plot pressure against oil produced. If the reservoir were sealed, rock and fluid expansion alone would have taken it to the bubble point after about a hundred thousand barrels.
pressure#3: Instead it produced two million barrels with almost no pressure loss. More than ninety nine percent of the voidage was replaced by water. The drive is a strong bottom-water aquifer. Recovery here is about sweep and water handling, not pressure, and every new well should be designed for low drawdown.
fluids#0: The fluids. The oil is light: twenty eight to thirty one degrees API in every analysis from 1956 to 2019, with one to one point seven percent sulphur. Reservoir temperature is about ninety eight degrees Celsius.
fluids#1: The gas is mostly methane, but sour: about eleven percent carbon dioxide and one to one point seven percent hydrogen sulphide. Sour-service materials are needed, and the gas is flared under the evaluation-period approval.
fluids#2: The gas situation: twenty seven years of production give a solution gas–oil ratio of about five fifty to five seventy standard cubic feet per barrel, and TEC-10 tested at about seven seventy. TEC-2’s first test, at the crest in 1956, is possible evidence of a small gas cap; field GOR stayed low for decades, so any gas cap was small. One flag: the flaring permit was justified at three thirty seven, below every measured value. That needs reconciling with the regulator.
fluids#3: And there has never been a laboratory PVT study. Every bubble point and formation volume factor in circulation is a correlation. TEC-12’s bottom-hole sample would be the field’s first.
core#0: The only core in the field is from TEC-10: ten metres cut in El Abra, one point three recovered, because the rock was so fractured it would not come out of its sleeve. Three plugs give two to eight percent porosity and well under a millidarcy of matrix permeability.
core#1: Yet the 2018 well tests need eighteen millidarcies at TEC-10 and about fifty at TEC-2. The oil flows through fractures and dissolution vugs. That is also why water moves fast and wells cone.
core#2: Two gaps worth noting: the upper window that TEC-12 targets has never been cored anywhere, and there are no capillary-pressure or relative-permeability data. Both are cheap to fix in the next well.
logs#0: These are TEC-10’s logs, drawn simply: gamma ray, resistivity, porosity and photo-electric factor against depth below sea level.
logs#1: The brown band is the marl, from two thousand two hundred and ninety four to two thousand three hundred and eleven metres. Resistivity is about five ohm-metres and the photo-electric factor is low: clay and quartz, not limestone.
logs#2: At about two thousand three hundred and eleven metres the curves change together. Resistivity jumps to fifteen to fifty ohm-metres and the photo-electric factor rises to limestone. That is the El Abra top. Tonalli perforated four metres just below it and the well tested one hundred and eighty two barrels a day.
logs#3: The yellow line is where the reef top is at TEC-12, seventeen metres higher. The interval that is marl at TEC-10 should be reef at the crest, and the well will log it before anything is perforated.
ooip#0: How much oil was there? Five estimates are in the files and each recomputes exactly from its own inputs. PEMEX and CNH booked seven point eight million barrels. IFR’s volumetric, which GLJ uses, is eleven point two. The independent Petrel Robertson model gives either answer depending on which logs it is fed.
ooip#1: Spanning those inputs, the range is eight to twelve million barrels, with ten as the P50.
ooip#2: Porosity and net-to-gross move the answer most, by about two and a half million barrels each way. Area and structure matter much less. So the gap is a petrophysics question, which modern logs in a new well can answer.
ooip#3: At the reef-rim average recovery, about nine hundred thousand barrels remain to be recovered, in a range of three hundred thousand to one point six million.
recovery#0: How does the recovery compare with other El Abra pools? This is the CNH table of forty five El Abra fields, recovery to date against the oil in place. Reef-rim fields have recovered a median of thirty percent; the best reach fifty. Tecolutla, in orange, has recovered about twenty five percent on the CNH volume, or eighteen on IFR’s larger volume.
recovery#1: Its nearest neighbours bracket it. Miguel Hidalgo, next door to the north-west, has recovered twenty two percent; Ignacio Allende, to the south-east, twenty seven; Vicente Guerrero thirty seven and Gutiérrez Zamora forty.
recovery#2: So on the CNH volume Tecolutla has done about what a typical small reef-rim pool does; on the IFR volume it is below the trend, with about a third of its trend recovery still ahead. Either way, the remaining oil is about nine hundred thousand barrels, and most of it sits at the crest.
opex#0: Operations. The green line is oil, the blue area is produced water, and orange is field operating cost per month. In 2018 and 2019, with TEC-10 and TEC-2 on, the field cost seventy to eighty thousand dollars a month to run.
opex#1: Then the costs came down by two thirds, to about twenty four thousand dollars a month in mid 2020, while oil held and water actually rose.
opex#2: The reason is water. From August 2019 the produced water went down TEC-7 as an injector instead of onto trucks, which ended trucking and disposal fees. Rented separators and pumps were returned, a flowline joined TEC-10 to TEC-2, and one supervision contract replaced the site engineers. After the 2022 shut-in the field cost twenty to fifty thousand dollars a month to hold.
costs#0: At its leanest, in September 2020, the field’s running cost was about twenty eight thousand dollars a month. Nearly half is the field crew and supervision, then a vacuum truck, diesel, tanks and sampling. Area charges add about five thousand two hundred a month.
costs#1: On capital, TEC-10 cost just under three million dollars all-in including its core, site and casing. The horizontal TEC-11 cost three and a half million on the tax basis, and up to four point four with completion invoices whose status is unresolved. The TEC-2 workovers came to under nine hundred thousand.
costs#2: TEC-12’s 2020 AFE was one point five seven million, which indexes to two point oh four million today. Because TEC-10 came in higher than its own budget, we carry a high case of two point two million.
current#0: So where does the field stand today? Nothing is producing. But two wells can come back.
current#1: TEC-10 is restorable. Its last steady rates were thirty to forty five barrels a day at seventy to eighty six percent water, and the reservoir behind it is at full pressure. It needs a solvent or hot-oil clean-up at restart and then a regular treatment schedule for wax, which is how it was run in 2019. TEC-2 can produce intermittently at sixteen to twenty three barrels a day alongside it.
current#2: TEC-7 remains the disposal well, and the rest are plugged or temporarily abandoned.
current#3: And TEC-12 is planned from the same pad as TEC-10, which means it shares the battery, the flowline and the disposal well. That is what makes it pay.
target#0: So to TEC-12, starting at the surface. These are the well pads. TEC-12 is drilled from the existing TEC-10 pad, beside the old TEC-6 location, so there is no new lease, road or flowline. From there it is a deviated S-shaped well: it kicks off and steps out about a hundred and seventy five metres east-north-east to the crest, finishing between TEC-6, TEC-9 and TEC-10.
target#1: Follow the well down. The target is the top of El Abra at the crest, about two thousand three hundred metres below sea level.
target#2: First, it has never been produced. Every crest well perforated below the top fourteen to twenty seven metres of the reef, chasing the water upward from below. Nothing anywhere has produced from minus two thousand two hundred and ninety four to minus two thousand three hundred and three.
target#3: Second, where that top unit has been logged it is oil-bearing. PEMEX’s 1957 electric log in TEC-7, run before any production, shows the top seven metres at thirteen percent water saturation and seventeen percent porosity. TEC-9, a hundred and eighteen metres away, shows its top eight metres porous and at the same saturation as the interval that made three hundred and fifty thousand barrels. PEMEX cemented it and never perforated it.
target#4: Third, it is the highest point on the seismic. So the target is the top eight metres or so of El Abra, reached fourteen to twenty metres higher than at TEC-10, with the proven interval below as the fallback.
design#0: The well itself is conventional: an S-shaped deviated well from the TEC-10 pad, about thirteen rig days, seven-inch casing to total depth.
design#1: What makes it an appraisal well is the data. Before anything is perforated it logs density, neutron, photo-electric factor, resistivity and an image across the whole window, takes formation pressures and a bottom-hole sample. The decision rule is simple: if the top unit shows low clay and hydrocarbon, perforate it; otherwise complete in the proven interval below.
design#2: The AFE is dominated by the rig, tubulars and mud. One point five seven million in 2020, two point oh four million today.
risks#0: The risks, and how the programme answers each one. The top unit could be thin or shaly, because the marl thickens off the crest. The logs answer that before completion.
risks#1: There may be a transition zone: in 2019 the operator thought the free-water level might have risen. Resistivity, pressures and the sample answer it, and nothing is perforated until they do.
risks#2: There was gas at the crest in 1956. Neutron–density and the sample answer that.
risks#3: Water coning is a certainty in this field, managed with low drawdown, in-field disposal and solvent clean-ups.
risks#4: And execution: TEC-11 lost its lateral, and TEC-6 on the same pad has a parted casing. TEC-12 is a conventional S-well with an anti-collision plan.
reserves#0: Reserves. GLJ has evaluated the field every year since 2018. At year-end 2025, for Kinjal, it carries three hundred and forty eight thousand barrels proved, nine hundred and three thousand proved plus probable, and one point three eight million possible.
reserves#1: There have been no producing reserves since 2022. Almost all of it is TEC-12, which GLJ books at two fifty, four hundred and five seventy eight thousand barrels.
reserves#2: Our own base case for TEC-12 is lower, two hundred and eighteen thousand barrels, because we calibrate on TEC-10’s actual decline. That is the number the economics use.
economics#0: Economics, on GLJ’s October 2026 price deck, at the realised eighty one percent of WTI, with the contract’s royalties and tax.
economics#1: The key distinction is incremental versus stand-alone. For an owner already running the field, with TEC-10 back on and carrying the battery, disposal and area charges, TEC-12 adds about point four seven million dollars of NPV before tax, pays out in twenty seven months, at a twenty nine percent rate of return.
economics#2: As a stand-alone project carrying the whole field’s costs it is negative, minus point five seven million. That is why TEC-10 and TEC-2 coming back on matters.
economics#3: Flat-price break-evens are sixty six dollars WTI incremental and eighty six stand-alone.
bridge#0: GLJ values the same well at about two point oh eight million. We can rebuild their number from ours, one assumption at a time. Price deck and timing are small. Their capex is a little lower. Their type well adds about half a million.
bridge#1: The big step, one and a half million, is operating cost: GLJ charges nothing for water handling, while we charge for water at forty to eighty five percent cut, as the actual 2020 and 2021 costs did. Both cases are internally consistent; ours is the more conservative.
netback#0: Here is the field’s commercial record under Tonalli, from the lease operating statements. The crude was trucked to PEMEX’s Central de Almacenamiento y Bombeo, the CAB Poza Rica, where it is measured on the fiscal meter and sold, through the Ezequiel Ordóñez pumping station at La Guásima, Papantla. Each bar is a year: royalties and fees, operating cost, and what was left. Over 2018 to 2023, revenue less royalties and opex is about zero, before overheads and seven point six million dollars of capital.
netback#1: Royalties and fees took forty one to fifty six percent of revenue. Put plainly: two watered-out wells could not carry the field.
netback#2: What changes the ratio is a well with a low water cut at the crest. More of the same water does not.
